model_interpretation.claim: Fusing the forward and input-gradient work into one launch should save launch overhead and reuse output coordinates, input bounds checks, and filter-base setup. The shared loop adds a second accumulator and loads for both paths, so register pressure or reduced occupancy may offset those savings; complete-call timing is needed to determine the result.

model_interpretation.claim: The measured same-thread fusion is correct and modestly faster than baseline (34.929 ms vs 35.464 ms, about 1.51%), but it keeps two accumulators and two input streams live per output thread. This contrasting launch-fused variant assigns separate, path-specialized block cohorts to y and gx: it retains one launch while reducing per-thread live state, at the cost of duplicated coordinate/bounds work and twice as many blocks. items.subject: Measure a fused forward and input-gradient kernel
items.objective: Own the forward/input-gradient execution path in src/candidate.cu. Test a fused kernel that computes y and gx together, sharing coordinate/filter handling where beneficial; measure whether fewer launches and shared work outweigh increased register use or reduced occupancy. Do not modify the weight-gradient path. Preserve full FP32, zero-padding semantics, all-input correctness and tolerances, complete fresh writes to both outputs, and the fixed API. Compare complete-call timing and report measured results rather than assuming fusion helps.
